title: A galactic embrace
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097 and its companion, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
celestial: NGC 1097 · constellation Fornax · about 50 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1097 seems to wrap its arms around a much smaller companion, the elliptical galaxy NGC 1097A, visible at the top left. The pair lies about 50 million light-years away in the constellation of Fornax, and there are signs that the two have interacted recently.

NGC 1097 is a Seyfert galaxy, which means a supermassive black hole sits at its centre. Its core is fairly faint, though, suggesting that the black hole is not currently consuming large amounts of gas and stars. The most striking feature at the centre is instead a ring of bright knots around the nucleus. Astronomers think these are huge bubbles of hydrogen gas glowing because ultraviolet light from young stars has ionised them, and they show that the ring is forming stars vigorously.
Bluish clusters of hot, young stars also dot the spiral arms.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (7.13 x 8.04 arcminutes) and distance (50 million light years), the frame spans roughly 104,000 × 117,000 light-years. Its light set out about 50 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The data come from the VIMOS instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, taken in visible light through three filters: R (652 nm) shown in red, V (540 nm) shown in green and B (456 nm) shown in blue. Colour information from an image by amateur astronomer Robert Gendler was added.

understand.eye: A telescope and long exposures collect far more light than the eye, which could not see the colours or the star-forming ring in such detail.

explore: NGC 1097 has four faint jets, too faint to show here, that form an X from its centre and are the longest visible-light jets known for any galaxy. They are thought to be the remains of a dwarf galaxy that NGC 1097 tore apart and swallowed, possibly as long as a few billion years ago. The knots in the ring are thought to be about 750–2500 light-years across.
alt: A spiral galaxy with a bright central ring and bluish star clusters in its arms, with a small elliptical galaxy at the top left.
